From camera to final print

HS Photography · eight lessons, every step drawn.

Welcome to the film journey

This guide takes you from loading a roll of film into a Pentax K1000 to holding your own final print. It follows the 8 HS Photography tutorial videos in the order they were uploaded, one lesson per video.

How to use this guide: watch the video first, then follow the numbered steps here while you practice. Each lesson ends with "Remember" tips that keep you, your film and the darkroom safe. Tap any plate to see it full size.

Lesson 1 · How to Load Film

You load the film when the frame counter reaches 1 and the rewind knob turns each time you advance.

  1. Open the back. Pull the rewind crank all the way up. The back cover pops open.
  2. Check the cassette. Hold it with the protruding nub pointing down and the flat end pointing up, then drop it in.
  3. Lock it in. Push the rewind knob back down so the cassette sits securely.
  4. Pull the leader across. Gently pull the film leader toward the take-up spool on the right.
  5. Hook the leader. Push the tip of the leader deep into one of the slots on the take-up spool.
  6. Advance slowly. Pull the advance lever. If it is locked, press the shutter button first.
  7. Check the teeth. The sprocket teeth must catch the holes on both the top and bottom edges of the film.
  8. Close the back. Press the cover shut until you hear a click.
  9. Wind to frame 1. Fire the shutter and advance one or two more times until the counter shows 1.

Remember

  • Watch the rewind knob on the left while you advance. It should rotate every time you advance; that shows the film is really moving.
  • Never force the advance lever. If it feels locked, press the shutter button first.

Lesson 2 · Meet the Pentax K1000

The Pentax K1000 is a fully manual film camera: you set every control yourself, and it will be your best friend in this class.

Where Part What it does
Lens Focus ring Turn it to make your subject sharp
Lens Aperture ring Controls how much light enters the camera (the f-stop)
Top plate Shutter speed dial Sets how long the shutter stays open
Top plate Film advance lever Moves the film to the next frame
Top plate Shutter button Takes your photo

Remember

  • Two rings live on the lens (focus, aperture). Three controls live on top (speed dial, advance lever, shutter button).
  • Aperture and shutter speed work together to control exposure. You will use both in Lesson 3.

Lesson 3 · How to Shoot

A light meter app on your phone measures the light and gives you the right shutter speed, so every frame comes out well exposed.

  1. Set the ISO. In the app, set the ISO to match the film you loaded.
  2. Choose your aperture. Pick the f-stop you want in the app.
  3. Meter your subject. Point your phone at the subject. The app calculates the shutter speed for you.
  4. Copy the numbers to the camera. Turn the shutter speed dial and the aperture ring to match the app.
  5. Focus. Look through the viewfinder and turn the focus ring until your subject is tack sharp.
  6. Shoot and advance. Press the shutter button, then pull the advance lever right away so you are ready for the next shot.

Remember

  • ISO in the app must match the ISO printed on your film box.
  • Make "shoot, then advance" a habit, so you never miss a moment.

Lesson 4 · How to Unload Film

Your roll is finished when the advance lever suddenly gets stuck and will not move. Do not force it. Rewind the film back into its cassette first.

  1. Press the rewind button. Turn the camera upside down and press the small rewind button on the bottom.
  2. Unfold the crank. Flip out the handle on the rewind crank.
  3. Rewind. Turn the crank clockwise, following the arrow.
  4. Feel for the release. Keep turning until the tension suddenly drops or you hear a faint click.
  5. Open and remove. Pull the rewind crank all the way up to open the back, then take out your film.

Remember

  • Never open the back before rewinding. Light would ruin the photos you just took.
  • The tension drop or click means the film is safely back inside the cassette.

Lesson 5 · Into the Reel

In this lesson you wind your film onto a developing reel in total darkness and seal it in a light-proof tank.

Meet the developing tank. It is a light-proof container where the chemistry happens. It comes in two sizes: a 2-reel tank and a 3-reel tank, depending on how many rolls you develop.

Tank part What it is for
Tank body Holds the reels and the chemicals
Center column The reels slide onto it; its flared base goes at the bottom
Reels Hold your film in a spiral so the chemicals reach every part
Light-tight funnel lid Lets chemicals in, keeps light out

Part A: with the lights on

  1. Pull out the leader. Pull about 2 in of film out of the cassette.
  2. Cut straight. Cut straight across between the sprocket holes, so no sharp plastic hooks are left.
  3. Snip the corners. Cut both corners at a 45° angle. This is the secret to stopping the film from jamming.
  4. Start the reel. Slide the trimmed edge into the reel's entry points, past the ball bearings, until you hear a soft click. Stop there. Do not wind the rest in the light.
  5. Organize your station. Put the center column in the tank, flared base all the way to the bottom. Upside down, it lets light leak in and ruins the film.
  6. Take your position. Stand with your back against the counter, waist touching the edge, reel and film in your hands. This keeps a safe path for teachers and assistants around the central sink.

Part B: lights off

  1. Pull the film out slowly from the cassette.
  2. Wind the reel. Hold it with both hands. Keep one hand still and twist the other side back and forth, step by step, to the end of the roll.
  3. Tear, don't cut. At the end, tear the film off the spool by hand. No scissors in the dark.
  4. Tuck in the tail. Advance the rest of the film fully into the reel tracks so it does not touch the tank walls.
  5. Load the tank. Feel for your tank and slide the reel down onto the center column. Sharing a tank? Wait for your partner, then stack their reel on top of yours.
  6. Seal it. Put on the lid and twist it closed. It must sit flat, not cross-threaded, and click firmly.

Remember

  • Film stuck in the dark? Don't panic. Call out for help and hold your reel straight out in front of you, so helpers can find your hands without bumping into you.
  • Once the lid clicks, your film is safely sealed from the light.

Lesson 6 · Film Development

Developing takes about 20 minutes of chemistry: developer 6 min, stop bath 1 min, fixer 5 min, wash 5 min, Photo-Flo 2 min. The amounts below are for a 2-reel tank (600 ml). Always measure for your own tank size.

Get ready

  1. Pre-wash. Fill the tank with water and pour it out.
  2. Use the right jug. Jugs are labeled water, developer, stop bath and fixer. Always use the matching jug to avoid contamination.
  3. Make 20 °C water. Get cold water from the drinking dispenser outside, then mix in tap water at the classroom sink until a thermometer reads exactly 20 °C.
  4. Mix the developer. Measure concentrated Ilford film developer in the small graduated cylinder: 20 ml, poured into the red jug. Add 580 ml of 20 °C water to reach 600 ml.

The chemical steps

Step Time Agitation (twist the rod left and right) When the timer ends
Developer 6 min Minute 1: continuously. Minutes 2–6: 3 twists at the start of each minute Pour down the sink, then rinse with tap water
Stop bath 1 min Continuously for the full minute Funnel it back into its gallon (reusable), then rinse
Fixer 5 min 3 twists at the start of each minute Funnel it back into its gallon (reusable)
Final wash 5 min Tank under running tap, overflowing Pour the water out
Photo-Flo 2 min Reels soak in the solution your IIA prepared Take the reels out

Dry your film

  1. Open the tank and take out the reels. Sharing? Give your partner their reel back.
  2. Unspool. Make a loose loop with your thumb and index (or middle) finger through the reel's center hole and gently pull the film end. The reel spins by itself.
  3. Squeegee. Gently run your index and middle fingers down the film to remove excess water.
  4. Label it. Write your name and period on a small piece of paper and clip it to the top of the film.
  5. Add a weight. Clip another clip to the very bottom to keep the film straight while it dries.
  6. Into the cabinet. Bring your film to the drying cabinet. Your IIA or teacher arranges the films so they don't touch.

Remember

  • When measuring from a gallon, always pour from the side to avoid bubbles and splashes into eyes or onto clothes.
  • Never let wet film touch the floor or any surface. It scratches and collects dust.

Lesson 7 · Contact Sheet Printing

A contact sheet prints all your frames on one sheet of photo paper, so you can choose which shots to enlarge. You make a test strip first to find the right exposure time.

Sleeve your negatives

  1. Once the film is completely dry, lay the archive sleeve flat, right way up.
  2. Leave the top row empty and slide your strips into the rows below.
  3. Use the edge of the sleeve as a cutting guide. No need to count frames.
  4. You should end with 24 frames, top and bottom rows empty. The empty space makes the sleeve easier to handle and align.

Know your enlarger and timer

Control What it does
Height knob Raises or lowers the enlarger head. Higher = wider light (bigger image) but dimmer
Focus knob Sharpens the projected light. Refocus every time you change the height
Lens aperture ring Opening = brighter light, closing = dimmer
White button Turns the light on continuously so you can set up
Red button Turns the light off
Green button Starts the timed exposure; the light switches off by itself
10x / 1x switch At 10x the dial number is multiplied by 10. At 1x the numbers are seconds

Make a test strip (under the safelight)

  1. Place a small strip of photo paper down. Lay the row of negatives with the most consistent exposure on top and lower the contact glass.
  2. Cover most of the strip with opaque cardboard, held at a slight diagonal so the exposure lines don't blend with straight lines in your photo.
  3. Slide the card across step by step, pressing start for each interval: 40, 20, 10, 5, 5 seconds. Leave the last section unexposed to check the paper is still good.
  4. Because light adds up, one strip now shows 0, 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 seconds.

Process the paper

Tray Time
Developer 1 min, agitate gently until the image appears
Stop bath 30 sec
Fixer at least 1 min
Pre-wash quick dip
Main wash (running water) 5 min

Lift with tongs and let it drip between trays. Then feed it through the print dryer: switch up to turn on, switch down as soon as you're done.

Print the full sheet

  1. In normal light, line up the dry test strip with the test strip exposure guide. Pick the section with the best contrast, rich blacks and clear details.
  2. Back under the safelight, turn on the focus light and place a dummy paper the same size as your photo paper. Make sure the light covers the whole sheet.
  3. Light off. Put the real photo paper on top of the dummy, lay your whole sleeve over it and lower the contact glass.
  4. Set your chosen time and press start to expose the whole sheet at once.
  5. Process it exactly like the test strip, then run it through the dryer.

Remember

  • Inspect each frame with a loupe for sharpness and composition, and circle your favorites with a grease pencil. Those are your final enlargements.

Lesson 8 · Final Print

Your final print is an enlargement of the one frame you circled on your contact sheet. The key rule for the carrier: dull side down, picture upside down.

Load the negative carrier

  1. Find your frame. Look at the frame you circled on your contact sheet and pull the matching strip from your negative sleeve.
  2. Take out the carrier. Slide the negative carrier out of the enlarger and open it on the table.
  3. Check both sides. Hold the strip by its edges. One side of the film is dull, the other is shiny.
  4. Dull side down, shiny side up. Lay the strip on the carrier with the dull side facing down.
  5. Turn it upside down. Flip the strip so your picture is upside down, center your frame in the window, and close the carrier.
  6. Put it back. Slide the carrier back into the enlarger.

Why upside down? The enlarger lens flips the image as it projects it. An upside-down negative in the carrier gives you a right-way-up picture on the paper. If you load it the right way up, your print comes out upside down.

Set up and focus

  1. Use a dummy paper. Under the safelight, put a dummy paper the same size as your real photo paper in the easel.
  2. Size the image. Turn on the enlarger light and use the height knob until the light covers the whole sheet.
  3. Focus on the grain. Place the grain focuser on the easel and look through it. Turn the focus knob until the tiny grains of the film look crisp. Sharp grain means a sharp print.
  4. Check and switch off. Remove the focuser, check your framing, then turn the light off.

Test strip

  1. Lay it across your subject. Place a strip of photo paper across the main subject of your picture, so you see the exposure on what matters most.
  2. Expose step by step. Cover most of it with the cardboard at an angle and expose it section by section, as in Lesson 7.
  3. Process and dry it, then compare it with the test strip exposure guide in normal light. Choose the time with the best contrast.

Print it

  1. Swap the paper. Back under the safelight, replace the dummy with a real sheet of photo paper and close the easel frame to hold it flat.
  2. Expose. Set your chosen time and press the green button.
  3. Process it the same way as before: developer, stop bath, fixer, wash and dry (times in Lesson 7).

Remember

  • Dull side down, picture upside down.
  • Refocus every time you change the height.
  • Put your test strip across the subject, not across empty sky or background.
